Title: A Comprehensive Benchmark Dataset for Sheet Metal Forming: Advancing Machine Learning and Surrogate Modelling in Pro-cess Simulations
Text:
A Comprehensive Benchmark Dataset for Sheet Metal Forming: 
Advancing Machine Learning and Surrogate Modelling in Pro-
cess Simulations 
Pascal Heinzelmann1*, Sebastian Baum2, Kim Rouven Riedmüller1, Mathias Liewald1, and Michael Weyrich2 
1Institute for Metal Forming Technology, University of Stuttgart, Holzgartenstraße 17, 70174 Stuttgart, Germany 
2Institute of Industrial Automation and Software Engineering, University of Stuttgart, Pfaffenwaldring 47, 70550 Stuttgart, Germany 
Abstract. FEM simulations are widely used for process development in the field of sheet metal forming to 
streamline tool design, shorten development cycles and minimize costly try-out processes. However, signif-
icant manual adjustments remain necessary due to deviations between simulation predictions and actual 
production outcomes, stemming from modelling simplifications. To further accelerate development cycles 
and try-out phases, it is essential to improve simulation accuracy and reduce computational demands. Here, 
surrogate models derived from simulation data by using machine learning provide a promising solution. In 
this context, the present paper introduces a comprehensive dataset designed to train surrogate models for 
optimizing sheet metal forming processes. The dataset includes extensive FE simulation data of deep-drawn 
sheet metal parts with an example geometry, considering diverse material and process parameters. It cap-
tures interactions among the tool geometry, material properties and process conditions, providing insights 
into stress distributions and strain paths. An example application demonstrates using the dataset to model 
the impact of material and process parameters on the forming limit diagram (FLD) of a deep-drawn part. 
The dataset, along with detailed documentation of the simulation setup, parameter scope and data formats, 
is available to the scientific community to facilitate further research in sheet metal forming optimization. 
Keywords: deep drawing; sheet metal forming; benchmark; FEM. 
1 Introduction 
Sheet metal forming is a fundamental manufacturing 
technology used in various industrial sectors such as au-
tomotive, aerospace and consumer goods production. 
This technology allows sheet metal materials to be 
formed into complex geometries with high precision and 
material efficiency, making it indispensable in modern 
production [1]. 
To further optimize and refine sheet metal forming 
processes, numerical simulations have become an essen-
tial tool in product development. [2] Such simulations 
allow engineers to analyse various aspects of the form-
ing process, e.g. material flow, stress and strain distribu-
tion in the formed component and failure prediction, 
without requiring costly and time-consuming physical 
experiments. As a result, the advanced computational 
models currently available enable manufacturers to re-
duce development time, minimize material waste and 
improve the overall quality of formed sheet metal com-
ponents [3]. 
However, the computational costs of these process 
simulations remain a major challenge. High-fidelity 
simulations require considerable computing resources 
and can take hours or even days, depending on the com-
plexity of the process considered. To address this issue,

artificial intelligence (AI) approaches have been ex-
plored as an alternative or surrogate for numerical sim-
ulation. In the field of sheet metal forming, AI tech-
niques have been applied to predict forming limit 
curves, optimize process parameters such as blank 
holder forces, and improve springback prediction [4]. AI 
models, particularly machine learning techniques, can 
approximate simulation results with sufficient accuracy 
while drastically reducing computing time. The models 
are trained using large datasets of precomputed simula-
tions, enabling them to predict forming outcomes in a 
fraction of the time required by conventional numerical 
methods [5].  
Despite their potential, AI-driven approaches are not 
yet widely adopted in the field of sheet metal forming 
due to the large amount of data required and a lack of IT 
expertise. The generation of training datasets requires 
extensive simulation efforts, consuming both time and 
computational power. In contrast, many other fields of 
AI research benefit from readily available datasets as 
benchmarks for tasks like image classification [6] or 
point cloud analysis [7]. These commonly available da-
tasets even enable newcomers to develop AI models and 
evaluate them against existing solutions. In sheet metal 
forming, however, such standardized datasets are rarely 
available. This not only prevents new research, but also

limits the reproducibility of published models, as they 
cannot be retrained or validated without access to the 
original data. 
To address these challenges and accelerate AI adop-
tion in sheet metal forming technology, a comprehen-
sive benchmark dataset (“Deep Drawing with LS-
DYNA” – see Appendix for a detailed description) com-
prising parametrized finite element (FE) simulations 
was made available in the scope of this paper. This da-
taset includes variations in process parameters, material 
properties and geometric configurations, providing a 
standardized foundation for developing and evaluating 
AI models. The dataset’s structure enables researchers 
to investigate complex relationships between design pa-
rameters and forming outcomes, while its format en-
sures reproducible research and model comparisons. 
Hence, this contribution provides a more efficient and 
accessible solution to AI-driven design methods for 
sheet metal forming and bridges the gap between tradi-
tional FE simulations and real-time predictive model-
ling. 
Furthermore, this contribution presents an introduc-
tory use case for which the dataset was utilized to ana-
lyse forming limit diagrams (FLD) for different geome-
tries and parameter sets. The FLD represents the major 
and minor strains of all elements in a simulation, provid-
ing a critical assessment of the formability of sheet metal 
materials to be processed. According to Keeler [8] and 
Goodwin [9], specific regions within the FLD indicate 
the likelihood of failure (cracks, wrinkles), making it a 
valuable tool for evaluating the feasibility of sheet metal 
forming processes.  
To provide this information, a machine learning al-
gorithm is implemented that can predict the probability 
distribution of FLD categories occurring for given 
punch geometries. The approach uses combined dy-
namic graph convolutional neural networks (DGCNN) 
[10] with a late fusion architecture [11] to incorporate 
material and process parameters into the classification 
framework. The model training employed the Jensen-
Shannon Divergence (JSD) [12] with weighted loss 
functions to ensure a balanced consideration of all FLD 
regions while emphasizing critical areas that are prone 
to cracking. 
The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 details 
the dataset creation and simulation setup, highlighting 
the available features in the dataset. Section 3 demon-
strates the practical use case of the dataset and discusses 
the results in Section 4. Finally, Section 5 concludes the 
paper with a summary of findings and directions for fu-
ture research.

based, deep drawing of the sheet metal material DP600

The tool surfaces were meshed using shell elements 
with varying edge lengths. Plane regions (top and bot-

length. Angled regions contained at least six elements, 
while the radii were discretized with a minimum of ten 
elements across the curvature. The rectangular blank 
was meshed with an element size of 1 mm. In the simu-
lation, fully integrated shell elements (ELFORM = 16) 
with seven integration points (NIP = 7) were used. Con-
tact between blank and tool surfaces was modelled using 
*CONTACT_FORMING_ONE_WAY_TO_SUR-
FACE. The static friction coefficient (FC) for the simu-
lations was parameterized for all interactions. Once the 
blank holder was closed, a constant, parameterized force 
(BF) was applied normally to the blank holder. The ma-
terial behaviour of the blank was modelled using 
*MAT_KINEMATIC_HARDENING_TRANS-
VERSELY_ANISOTROPIC. This material model com-
bines Yoshida’s and Uemori’s nonlinear kinematic 
hardening rule, as proposed in [13] with material type 
MAT 125, which is designed for simulating sheet metal 
forming processes with anisotropic material. Yoshida’s 
and Uemori’s theory utilizes two surfaces to describe the 
hardening behaviour: the yield surface and the bounding 
surface. During deformation, the yield surface translates 
without changing size, while the bounding surface 
evolves in both size and position. Within this material 
model, the material type MAT 125 specifically accounts 
for transverse anisotropy and allows for an optional load 
curve to define an arbitrary dependency of stress and ef-
fective plastic strain. This enhances the model’s ability 
to capture complex material behaviour in sheet metal 
forming processes. The anisotropic plasticity criterion 
behind material type MAT 125 is based on a yield func-
tion that captures the directional behaviour of materials 
under stress. The anisotropic constants of the model are 
typically obtained by experimental testing and numeri-
cal calibration. This process involves using test data 
(tensile, compression, shear and multiaxial tests) to 
identify material properties, followed by numerical op-
timisation to fit the parameters in LS-DYNA. Full cali-
bration of the model is an iterative process that ensures 
the material behaviour is accurately captured for a range 
of loading conditions. 
To account for material variability, the hardening 
factor was scaled by a parameter (MAT) representing 
material scatter. Consequently, for each geometry, all 
parameters permutation were simulated. Additionally, 
the sheet metal thickness (SHTK) was varied as well. 
All variations made for the parameters are shown in. So, 
each geometry had 5,346 parameter sets, which leads to 
a total of 32,076 simulations. Each simulation run took 
about 1.5 hours on an AMD EPYC 7742 CPU.

As part of the study described in this paper, an ex-
ample use case was provided demonstrating how the ob-
tained dataset can be utilized. The dataset contains the 
simulation data of a deep-drawing process and an addi-
tional springback, including stresses, strains, thick-
nesses per element and nodal displacements (as shown 
for the final step of the deep-drawing process in Fig. 3). 
In addition to these data, the geometries and parameters 
used for each simulation were also recorded. 
Although there exist APIs for working with the 
d3plot simulations, in terms of execution speed it is rec-
ommended to first extract the desired information and 
convert it into a faster file format. Therefore, each sim-
ulation is marked with a unique ID, which is equal to the 
file name of the HDF5 file. In the metadata of a HDF5 
file the corresponding geometry, process and material 
parameters is added, thus enabling that all necessary in-
formation and data of one simulation to be retrieved 
from one file (for full data description please see Appen-
dix).  
3 Benchmark Example Use Case 
The use case utilizes the Forming Limit Diagram (FLD) 
(see Fig. 4) to analyse the simulated deep-drawing pro-
cess. The FLD represents the major and minor strain val-
ues of all elements in a simulation and indicates the fea-
sibility of a sheet metal forming process without failure. 
Depending on the relationship between the major and 
minor strains, different forming regions can be identi-
fied. Elements above the forming limit curve (FLC) are 
in the failure zone (red), indicating potential rupture, 
while those in the excessive thinning zone are at risk of 
localized necking. 
The magenta area indicates wrinkling, which occurs 
when the ratio of major to minor strain is less than -1.

area above the FLC. A shifted FLC with a 10 % reduc-

where elements are at risk of cracking. For an element 
to be considered safe, it must be within the green area, 
which is below the yellow area and above the blue area. 
The small grey area near the FLD’s origin surrounding 
these regions represents inadequately strained elements 
that have not experienced a major strain reduction 
greater than 0.02.

For the investigations on the present use case, each 
element in every simulation carried out was analysed to 
determine its position within these regions, allowing for 
the classification based on their forming behaviour of 
the simulations. For the example shown in Fig. 4, the 
elements were colour-coded based on their position in 
the FLD. The results of the example indicate that this 
simulation exhibits four categories: “Wrinkles”, “Wrin-
kling tendency”, “Safe”, and “Inadequate stretch”. This 
classification was subsequently applied to the elements 
of all geometries and across all parameter combinations. 
To generate the FLD for a simulation, the major and 
minor strains for each element must be calculated from 
the strain tensor. The element strain tensor consists of a 
6 × 1 vector for each element. These six entries repre-
sent the symmetric strain tensor components: εxx, εyy, εzz, 
γxy, γyz, and γzx. The deformed part after the deep-draw-
ing process is considered relevant for this analysis. 
Since the strain tensor is presented in the global coordi-
nate system, an additional transformation into the re-
spective element coordinate system is necessary before 
calculating the major and minor strains. After transform-
ing the vectors into the element coordinate system, z-
components of the strain tensor were ignored due to the 
plane stress condition. From the resulting 2 × 2 matrix, 
eigenvalues were determined, representing the major 
and minor strains needed for the FLD.

gories, a discrete probability distribution is constructed 
by computing the relative frequency of elements in each 
category. Specifically, for each FLD category 𝑖𝑖, the ratio

To account for material and process parameters in 
the classification, both the reference geometry (repre-
sented as a point cloud X ∈ℝ𝑛𝑛×3) and the standardized 
parameters p ∈ℝ4 (see  
Table 2) is considered. Each parameter in p is stand-
ardized with zero mean and standard deviation equals to 
1 to prevent label shifting. Therefore, the classification 
task is formulated as y = fθ (X;p), with fθ denotes the 
classifier with a set of learnable parameters θ. The used 
implementation enhances the Dynamic Graph CNN 
(DGCNN) architecture [10] with a late fusion approach 
[11]. This enhancement concatenates the parameter vec-
tor p at the first fully connected layer of the DGCNN, 
enabling multimodal classification. The network pro-
cesses the point cloud data through edge convolution 
layers while simultaneously handling the metadata vec-
tor of relevant parameters.  
Rather than using one-hot encoded labels, the train-
ing approach applied utilizes complete probability dis-
tributions. This preserves the nuanced distribution of 
FLD categories and allows the model to learn the full 
spectrum of possible classifications for each input and 
represent the occurrences of all FLD categories. To ad-
dress the inherent class imbalance (Fig. 4) in FLD cate-
gories - particularly critical for rare but important cases 
such as cracks - weight factors wi are calculated for each 
category i, derived from the occurrence of each category 
in total: wi = 1 / f (yi), where f denotes the occurrence of 
class yi over the whole dataset.

The model is implemented using Pytorch based on 
the code provided by [10]. The point cloud data was 
standardized to 500 points per geometry. The DGCNN 
is trained with kNN = 8. The parameter vector is concat-
enated at the first fully connected layer (dim: 1024+5), 
followed by 2 additional fully connected layers. The da-
taset is split into training (80 %), validation (10 %) and 
test (10 %) sets according to [10], where the model is 
trained on the training set and evaluated on the test set. 
The training is conducted using the Adam optimizer 
with an initial learning rate of 0.001 and momentum of 
0.9. A batch size of 64 is employed and training was per-
formed for 250 epochs with early stopping based on val-
idation loss with a patience of 5 epochs. To prevent 
overfitting, a dropout of 50 % is applied during training. 
4 Results and discussion 
The training and test loss curves of the machine learning 
model, shown in Fig. 5 (left), demonstrate consistent 
convergence without signs of overfitting. The test loss 
exhibits spikes at the beginning of the training. These 
spikes are reason form to the weighted loss function, 
which emphasizes error cases more heavily than normal 
cases. These error cases weight in small batch sizes 
more than in the training batch size. While these spikes 
might suggest that the weighting scheme is numerical 
instable, they do not impact the overall learning process 
in later epochs.  
The probability distribution of predicted element 
states across all simulations reveals interesting patterns 
(see Fig. 5, middle and right). While the general struc-
ture mirrors the ground truth distribution, the applied 
model shows increased sensitivity to crack formation 
(3 % higher prediction rate). This bias towards predict-
ing failure modes may initially appear conservative, but 
it aligns with practical requirements in sheet metal form-
ing, where false negatives are more costly than false 
positives. However, further investigation is needed to 
determine if this conservative prediction tendency 
achieves an optimal balance between safety and practi-
cal utility. 
The model achieved convergence with final valida-
tion loss decreasing from initial values above 10 to be-
low 0.4. These results validate the weighted training ap-
proach, which successfully balances the need to accu-
rately predict both common and critical rare cases. The 
performance metrics indicate that the model can effec-
tively distinguish between different failure modes based 
on the punch geometry and the process-/material param-
eters while maintaining high accuracy for normal form-
ing conditions. 
To evaluate generalization capability, the trained 
model is cross-validated using a simulation that is not 
present in the generated dataset. The FLD (Fig. 6 left)

5 Conclusions 
The presented benchmark dataset represents a signifi-
cant contribution to AI-driven surrogate models for 
sheet metal forming processes. This work establishes a 
foundation for comparing surrogate modelling ap-
proaches and accelerating process development cycles 
by providing comprehensive FEA simulation data and 
detailed documentation. The dataset’s practical utility is 
illustrated through the classification of forming limit di-
agrams by showing how surrogate models can effec-
tively predict material behaviour under various forming 
conditions.  
While the results demonstrate the benchmark's 
value, limitations in geometric generalisation need to be 
considered for future applications as machine learning 
models can only make predictions within the parameter 
space of their training data. Cross-validation with an un-
seen simulation featuring significant crack formation 
demonstrated that while the model correctly identified 
the critical failure mode, it underestimated the crack 
prevalence by approximately 5 % and has deviation 
across lower priority classes. This highlights both the 
potential and limitations of surrogate models when con-
fronted with extreme cases outside the training distribu-
tion. Here, two primary directions for future research 
can be identified. First, the investigation of transfer 
learning approaches to extend the model's applicability 
and generalizability to new geometries and process con-
ditions. Second, the application of explainable AI tech-
niques to validate that multi-modal classification meth-
ods effectively utilize all available parameter infor-
mation. These advancements will further strengthen the 
connection between simulation and physical forming 
processes by incorporating real production measure-
ments to validate and refine simulation-based predic-
tions, ultimately supporting a more efficient and reliable 
development of sheet metal forming processes.

Abstract: FEM simulations are widely used for process development in the field of sheet metal forming to streamline tool design, shorten development cycles and minimize costly try-out processes. However, signif- icant manual adjustments remain necessary due to deviations between simulation predictions and actual production outcomes, stemming from modelling simplifications. To further accelerate development cycles and try-out phases, it is essential to improve simulation accuracy and reduce computational demands. Here, surrogate models derived from simulation data by using machine learning provide a promising solution. In this context, the present paper introduces a comprehensive dataset designed to train surrogate models for optimizing sheet metal forming processes. The dataset includes extensive FE simulation data of deep-drawn sheet metal parts with an example geometry, considering diverse material and process parameters. It cap- tures interactions among the tool geometry, material properties and process conditions, providing insights into stress distributions and strain paths. An example application demonstrates using the dataset to model the impact of material and process parameters on the forming limit diagram (FLD) of a deep-drawn part. The dataset, along with detailed documentation of the simulation setup, parameter scope and data formats, is available to the scientific community to facilitate further research in sheet metal forming optimization.
